description: Why do things move? Dive into Sir Isaac Newton's three laws and discover the invisible forces shaping the universe.

slides.title: Welcome to the Laws of Motion
slides.content:
# The Cause of Motion

In Kinematics, we learned how to describe motion (velocity, acceleration). But we never asked *why* things move, or why they stop moving.

To move a football at rest, someone must kick it. To throw a stone upwards, one has to give it an upward push.

It seems that an external **force** is needed to set a body in motion or to stop it.

## What You Will Learn:
- **Aristotle's Fallacy:** The ancient mistake.
- **Newton's Three Laws:** The foundation of classical mechanics.
- **Inertia and Momentum:** Mass in motion.
- **Friction:** The force that opposes motion.

slides.title: Aristotle's Fallacy
slides.content:
# The Old Belief

The Greek thinker Aristotle held the view that an external force is required to *keep* a body in uniform motion.

If you shoot an arrow, Aristotle thought the air pushing from behind kept it moving. If you slide a toy car, it stops because there's no force pushing it anymore.

For 2000 years, everyone believed this: "The natural state of a body is to be at rest."

But Aristotle was **wrong**. He didn't understand the invisible force of friction!

slides.title: Galileo and Inertia
slides.content:
# The New Truth

Galileo Galilei observed objects moving on inclined planes. He realized that if a surface was perfectly smooth (zero friction), an object moving on a horizontal plane would never stop!

> "The natural state of a body is to keep doing whatever it is already doing."

This property of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or uniform motion is called **inertia**.
- A heavier object (more mass) has more inertia than a lighter one.

slides.title: Inertia Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of Galileo's concept.
slides.quizQuestion: Which property of matter is a direct measure of its inertia?

slides.title: Newton's First Law of Motion
slides.content:
# The Law of Inertia

Sir Isaac Newton built on Galileo's ideas and formulated his First Law:

> **"Everybody continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to act otherwise."**

If the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero. 
Acceleration can be non-zero only if there is a net external force on the body.

*Example:* When a bus starts suddenly, you fall backward. Your lower body moves with the bus, but your upper body's *inertia* tries to remain at rest!

slides.title: Momentum
slides.content:
# Mass in Motion

To understand the Second Law, we first need to define a new quantity.

Imagine a ping-pong ball and a cricket ball hitting you at the exact same speed. Which one hurts more? The cricket ball, because it has more mass.
Now imagine two cricket balls, one tossed gently, one bowled at 150 km/h. The fast one hurts more because it has more velocity.

The impact of a body depends on BOTH its mass and its velocity. Newton defined a quantity called **Momentum (p)**:
`p = m * v`

Momentum is a vector quantity.

slides.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
slides.content:
# The Famous Equation

Newton's Second Law relates force to momentum:

> **"The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts."**

`F = dp / dt`
Since `p = mv`, if mass is constant, `F = m * (dv/dt)`.
And since `dv/dt` is acceleration (`a`), we get the most famous equation in mechanics:

`F = m * a`
(Force = Mass x Acceleration).

slides.title: Understanding F = ma
slides.content:
# Using the Second Law

`F = m * a` tells us that:
1. If you apply the same force to a light object and a heavy object, the light object will accelerate much faster.
2. To make a heavy object accelerate as fast as a light object, you need a much bigger force.

## The Unit of Force:
The SI unit of force is the **Newton (N)**.
1 Newton is the force required to accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s^2. 
`(1 N = 1 kg m s^-2)`.

slides.title: Force Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of the Second Law.
slides.quizQuestion: If you push a 5 kg box and it accelerates at 2 m/s^2, what is the net force acting on the box?

slides.title: Impulse
slides.content:
# The Sudden Force

Sometimes a very large force acts for a very short time, like a bat hitting a cricket ball.

In these cases, it's hard to measure the force and time separately. We measure their product, called **Impulse**.

`Impulse = Force * time duration = Change in momentum`

*Application:* A cricketer lowers his hands while catching a ball. By increasing the time it takes to stop the ball, he decreases the Force on his hands (since Change in momentum is constant)!

slides.title: Newton's Third Law of Motion
slides.content:
# Action and Reaction

Forces never occur alone in nature. They always occur in pairs.

> **"To every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction."**

- If body A exerts a force on body B, then body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A.
- **Important:** Action and reaction forces act on *different* bodies, not the same body. Therefore, they do NOT cancel each other out!

slides.title: Examples of the Third Law
slides.content:
# Rockets and Walking

How do we walk?
When you walk, you push the ground backward (Action). The ground pushes you forward with an equal and opposite force (Reaction). It is the ground's reaction force that moves you forward!

How does a rocket fly in space where there is no air to push against?
The rocket pushes the exhaust gases out the back with massive force (Action). The exhaust gases push the rocket forward with equal force (Reaction)!

slides.title: Conservation of Momentum
slides.content:
# Before and After the Crash

From the Second and Third Laws, we get a powerful principle:

> **The Law of Conservation of Momentum:** In an isolated system (where no external net force acts), the total momentum of the system remains constant.

If two cars crash into each other:
The momentum of Car A + Car B *before* the crash is exactly equal to the momentum of Car A + Car B *after* the crash. The momentum is just transferred between them!

slides.title: Friction
slides.content:
# The Invisible Opponent

Remember Aristotle's mistake? He forgot about friction.

When a body moves over another surface, a force opposes the relative motion. This force is called **friction**.

1. **Static Friction:** The force that prevents an object from moving when you first push it. It increases as you push harder, up to a maximum limit.
2. **Kinetic (Sliding) Friction:** Once the object starts moving, the friction drops slightly to a constant value. 

*Rule:* Kinetic friction is always slightly less than maximum static friction.

slides.title: Rolling Friction
slides.content:
# The Wheel's Secret

Why did humanity invent the wheel?

Because **Rolling Friction** is dramatically smaller than sliding (kinetic) friction!

When a wheel rolls without slipping, the point of contact with the ground is momentarily at rest. There is almost no sliding. This is why it is vastly easier to pull a heavy suitcase on wheels than to drag it across the floor. 

We also use ball bearings in machines to convert sliding friction into rolling friction to reduce wear and tear.

slides.title: Friction Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of friction types.
slides.quizQuestion: Which of the following forces of friction is generally the smallest in magnitude?

slides.title: Reviewing Key Terms
slides.content:
# Key Vocabulary Review

Let's lock in these critical terms:

- **Inertia:** The tendency of a body to resist changes in its motion (depends on Mass).
- **Momentum (p):** Mass times Velocity (p = mv).
- **Newton's 1st Law:** Objects keep doing what they are doing unless a force acts on them.
- **Newton's 2nd Law:** Force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma).
- **Newton's 3rd Law:** Every action has an equal and opposite reaction (acting on different bodies).
- **Impulse:** Force times time (equals the change in momentum).
- **Friction:** A force that opposes relative motion between surfaces.

slides.title: Topic Summary
slides.content:
# Summary of Laws of Motion

Excellent work! Here is a recap of what we've learned:

- Galileo corrected Aristotle by defining **Inertia**: objects in motion stay in motion without an external force.
- **Newton's 1st Law** formalizes inertia. 
- **Newton's 2nd Law** states that the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the force applied, giving us the formula **F = ma**.
- **Newton's 3rd Law** states that forces come in equal and opposite pairs (Action/Reaction).
- If no external force acts on a system, its total momentum is **conserved**.
- **Friction** opposes motion. Rolling friction is much less than kinetic friction, which is less than static friction.
